theory.intro: A **test** is the least information that guarantees a quadrilateral is a particular special shape. To prove a test, use congruent triangles; to apply one, match the given facts to a test and name it.
facts: A quadrilateral is a **parallelogram** if both pairs of opposite sides are equal, or both pairs of opposite angles are equal.
It is also a parallelogram if the diagonals bisect each other, or if **one pair** of opposite sides is equal **and** parallel.
A quadrilateral is a **rhombus** if all four sides are equal, a parallelogram has two adjacent sides equal, or the diagonals bisect at right angles.
A parallelogram is a **rectangle** if its diagonals are equal, and a **square** if it is both a rhombus and a rectangle.
**One pair** of opposite sides equal is not enough for a parallelogram, because an isosceles trapezium also fits.
One pair of sides parallel with the other pair equal is not enough either.
To prove a test, prove two triangles congruent, then use equal **alternate** angles to show that sides are parallel.
steps: Read the marked or given information: equal sides, equal or parallel sides, or facts about the diagonals.
Choose the test whose conditions exactly match that information, or set up congruent triangles to prove the test.
State the conclusion naming the test, and for a rhombus, rectangle or square, add the extra condition that upgrades the parallelogram.

foundation.solution_text:
In $\triangle ABC$ and $\triangle CDA$:
$AB = CD$ (given)
$BC = DA$ (given)
$AC$ is common.
$\therefore \triangle ABC \cong \triangle CDA$ (SSS)
$\therefore \angle BAC = \angle DCA$ (matching angles of congruent triangles)
These are equal alternate angles, so $AB \parallel DC$.
$\therefore \angle BCA = \angle DAC$ (matching angles of congruent triangles)
These are equal alternate angles, so $AD \parallel BC$.
Both pairs of opposite sides are parallel, so $ABCD$ is a parallelogram.

In $\triangle ABE$ and $\triangle CDE$:
$AE = CE$ (given, the diagonals bisect each other)
$BE = DE$ (given, the diagonals bisect each other)
$\angle AEB = \angle CED$ (vertically opposite angles)
$\therefore \triangle ABE \cong \triangle CDE$ (SAS)
$\therefore \angle BAE = \angle DCE$ (matching angles of congruent triangles)
These are equal alternate angles, so $AB \parallel DC$.
In the same way $\triangle ADE \cong \triangle CBE$ gives $AD \parallel BC$.
Both pairs of opposite sides are parallel, so $ABCD$ is a parallelogram.

In $\triangle ABC$ and $\triangle CDA$:
$AB = CD$ (given)
$\angle BAC = \angle DCA$ (alternate angles, $AB \parallel DC$)
$AC$ is common.
$\therefore \triangle ABC \cong \triangle CDA$ (SAS)
$\therefore \angle BCA = \angle DAC$ (matching angles of congruent triangles)
These are equal alternate angles, so $AD \parallel BC$.
Both pairs of opposite sides are parallel, so $ABCD$ is a parallelogram.

Both pairs of opposite angles are equal, which is the opposite-angles test for a parallelogram.
The four angles add to $360^{\circ}$, so $\angle A + \angle B = 180^{\circ}$; these are co-interior angles, so $AD \parallel BC$.
Similarly $\angle B + \angle C = 180^{\circ}$ gives $AB \parallel DC$.
Both pairs of opposite sides are parallel, so $ABCD$ is a parallelogram.

$AB = CD$ and $AD = BC$, so both pairs of opposite sides are equal.
A quadrilateral with both pairs of opposite sides equal is a parallelogram.
$ABCD$ is a parallelogram with two adjacent sides equal ($AB = AD$).
A parallelogram with two adjacent sides equal is a rhombus.
So $ABCD$ is a rhombus.

foundation.question_text:
A quadrilateral $ABCD$ has one pair of opposite sides equal, $AB = DC$.
A student claims this proves $ABCD$ is a parallelogram.
Explain why the claim is wrong.
foundation.solution_text:
One pair of opposite sides equal is not enough.
An isosceles trapezium has one pair of equal sides but only one pair of parallel sides, so it is not a parallelogram.
A valid test needs both pairs of opposite sides equal, or the equal pair to also be parallel.
So $AB = DC$ alone does not prove a parallelogram.

development.solution_text:
Because the diagonals bisect each other, $ABCD$ is a parallelogram.
In $\triangle ABE$ and $\triangle CBE$:
$AE = CE$ (given)
$\angle AEB = \angle CEB = 90^{\circ}$ (given, diagonals meet at right angles)
$BE$ is common.
$\therefore \triangle ABE \cong \triangle CBE$ (SAS)
$\therefore AB = CB$ (matching sides of congruent triangles)
A parallelogram with two adjacent sides equal is a rhombus.
So $ABCD$ is a rhombus.

$AE = CE$ (the diagonals bisect each other)
$3x - 2 = x + 8$
$2x = 10$
$x = 5$
Since $AE = CE$ and $BE = DE$, the diagonals bisect each other, so $ABCD$ is a parallelogram.

This is not enough to prove a parallelogram.
$AB \parallel DC$ is one pair of parallel sides, and $AD = BC$ are the non-parallel sides.
An isosceles trapezium fits this description exactly but is not a parallelogram.
The one-pair test needs the same pair to be both equal and parallel, that is $AB = DC$ as well.

$ABCD$ is already a parallelogram, and its diagonals are equal.
A parallelogram whose diagonals are equal is a rectangle.
So $ABCD$ is a rectangle (equal-diagonals test).

The diagonals of a parallelogram bisect each other, so $AE = CE$.
In $\triangle ABE$ and $\triangle CBE$:
$AE = CE$ (diagonals of a parallelogram bisect each other)
$\angle AEB = \angle CEB = 90^{\circ}$ (given, diagonals meet at right angles)
$BE$ is common.
$\therefore \triangle ABE \cong \triangle CBE$ (SAS)
$\therefore AB = CB$ (matching sides of congruent triangles)
A parallelogram with two adjacent sides equal is a rhombus.
So $ABCD$ is a rhombus.

$AB = BC$ (all sides of a rhombus are equal)
$3x - 1 = x + 5$
$2x = 6$
$x = 3$
$AB = 3(3) - 1 = 8$
So each side of the rhombus is $8$ cm.

mastery.solution_text:
The diagonals bisect each other, so $ABCD$ is a parallelogram.
In $\triangle AEB$ and $\triangle AED$:
$BE = DE$ (the diagonals bisect each other)
$\angle AEB = \angle AED = 90^{\circ}$ (diagonals meet at right angles)
$AE$ is common.
$\therefore \triangle AEB \cong \triangle AED$ (SAS)
$\therefore AB = AD$ (matching sides of congruent triangles)
A parallelogram with two adjacent sides equal is a rhombus.
So $ABCD$ is a rhombus.

$PR = QS$ (the diagonals are equal)
$4a = a + 9$
$3a = 9$
$a = 3$
The diagonals bisect each other, so $PQRS$ is a parallelogram; they are also equal, so $PQRS$ is a rectangle.

The diagonals bisect each other, so $ABCD$ is a parallelogram.
The diagonals bisect each other at right angles, so $ABCD$ is a rhombus (all sides equal).
The diagonals are equal, so the parallelogram is a rectangle (all angles right angles).
A quadrilateral that is both a rhombus and a rectangle is a square.
So $ABCD$ is a square.
